introduction-when-kubectl-logs-isnt-enou.core: Logs show what an app chose to say; many problems need more: inspecting a running distroless container, profiling CPU or memory, tracing DNS, or capturing packets. Kubernetes offers ephemeral debug containers, node debugging, port-forwarding to profiling endpoints and in-namespace packet capture to investigate without redeploying.

first_principles.problem: A distroless Pod has no shell, logs are unhelpful and the issue disappears on restart.
truths: Debug tools can be attached at runtime.

analogy.title: A doctor's diagnostic toolkit beyond asking 'how do you feel?'
analogy.story: Stethoscopes, scans and blood tests reveal what the patient can't describe.
analogy.breaks: Patients can't be cloned; you can copy a Pod for debugging with kubectl debug --copy-to.

check.q: Why avoid restarting a misbehaving Pod immediately?
check.a: Restarting can destroy the state and evidence needed to find the root cause.

kubectl-debug-the-ghost-in-the-shell.core: kubectl debug adds an ephemeral container to a running Pod (with tools like busybox, netshoot) that can share the target container's process namespace (--target) to inspect processes, files via /proc/<pid>/root and network. It can also copy a Pod with changes (--copy-to, --set-image) or debug a node (kubectl debug node/…) with host access.

first_principles.problem: A distroless container misbehaves and there's no shell or tools to inspect it.
truths: Ephemeral containers can join running Pods.
Process namespace sharing exposes the target's processes.
derivation: Use **kubectl debug node/x** for host issues.

analogy.title: A specialist entering the room through a side door
analogy.story: They bring their own tools without disturbing the patient.
analogy.breaks: Specialists leave when done; ephemeral containers stay in the Pod spec until the Pod is replaced.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Full toolbox next to a tool-less container.

code.text:
kubectl debug -it api-7f9 --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=api
# inside:
ps aux
ls /proc/1/root/etc/config
ss -tlnp
curl -s localhost:8080/health

check.q: What does --target do in kubectl debug?
check.a: Shares the process namespace with the specified container so you can see and inspect its processes.

profiling-x-raying-the-cpu-with-pprof.core: Profilers show where an app spends CPU, allocates memory or blocks. Go's net/http/pprof exposes /debug/pprof endpoints; you port-forward and fetch CPU, heap, goroutine and mutex profiles, then view flame graphs with go tool pprof. Other languages have equivalents (async-profiler, py-spy), and continuous profilers (Pyroscope, Parca) collect profiles in production.

first_principles.problem: A service burns 4 CPUs after a release, and nobody knows which function is responsible.
truths: Metrics show that CPU is high, not why.

analogy.title: An X-ray of where effort goes
analogy.story: You see exactly which bone is broken instead of guessing from the limp.
analogy.breaks: X-rays are one snapshot; profiles sample over a time window, so pick it during the problem.

example.title: CPU profile

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: 60% CPU in JSON re-encoding inside a loop.

code.text:
kubectl port-forward pod/api-7f9 6060:6060 &
go tool pprof -http=:8081 http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30

example.outcome: root cause in code, not guesses.

check.q: What does a CPU flame graph show?
check.a: Which call stacks consume the most CPU time, with wider frames meaning more time.

debugging-dns-tracing-the-infinite-loop.core: DNS issues cause timeouts and intermittent failures: ndots:5 search-domain expansion multiplies queries, CoreDNS overload or conntrack races drop UDP packets (5-second delays), forwarding loops (CoreDNS forwarding to itself via node resolv.conf) crash CoreDNS, and NetworkPolicies may block port 53. Trace from inside the Pod and check CoreDNS logs and metrics.

first_principles.problem: Requests intermittently take exactly 5 seconds longer, and CoreDNS keeps restarting with 'Loop detected'.
derivation: Check **loop plugin** errors and node resolv.conf.

analogy.title: A phone directory that keeps forwarding you to itself
analogy.story: You're put on hold, transferred back to reception, and so on forever.
analogy.breaks: Phone loops are obvious; DNS loops show as crashes and timeouts.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Point CoreDNS forward at real upstream; deploy NodeLocal DNSCache.

code.text:
kubectl exec -it client -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
kubectl exec -it client -- dig +search +all api.example.com
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns | grep -i loop

points: Watch for loops and 5 s delays.

check.q: What often causes exactly 5-second DNS delays in Kubernetes?
check.a: Dropped UDP DNS packets (e.g. conntrack races) triggering the resolver's 5-second retry timeout.

network-packet-inspection-with-tcpdump-a.core: To see actual traffic, run tcpdump in the Pod's network namespace: via an ephemeral netshoot container (shares the Pod network), from the node using nsenter -t <pid> -n, or with kubectl sniff / ksniff to stream captures into Wireshark. Filter tightly, capture briefly, and remember TLS hides payloads but not handshakes and flags.

first_principles.problem: Two services disagree about whether requests are even being sent.
truths: Pods share a network namespace across containers.
Captures can be large and sensitive.

analogy.title: Putting a microphone on the phone line
analogy.story: You hear exactly what was said and whether anyone answered.
analogy.breaks: Phone recordings are audio; packet captures may contain secrets, so handle them carefully.

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: SYN sent, RST returned: DB port closed on the target.

code.text:
kubectl debug -it api-7f9 --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- tcpdump -i eth0 -nn port 5432 -c 50
# or from the node:
nsenter -t $(crictl inspect --output go-template --template '{{.info.pid}}' <cid>) -n tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/api.pcap

check.q: Why can an ephemeral debug container capture a Pod's traffic?
check.a: It shares the Pod's network namespace, seeing the same interfaces and packets.
